title: Swapping two concepts in lens coordinates
takeaway: These three expressions define the paper's concept-exchange surgery: read how much of a source concept and a target concept an activation carries along their two J-lens directions, exchange those two numbers, and write the difference back. Everything the activation carries outside the plane spanned by the two lens vectors is left exactly as it was, so the edit swaps one concept for another rather than replacing the activation.
walkthrough:
The article prints no numbered equation here. The three expressions appear inside a sentence in the methods section, and together they specify the [[lens-coordinate-swap]] used in every swap experiment in the paper.

The first expression builds the matrix. A source token $s$ and a target token $t$ are chosen — France and China, say, or spider and ant. Each has a [[j-lens-vector]] at the layer being edited: a direction in [[residual-stream]] space that, averaged over contexts, disposes the model to say that token. Those two vectors become the columns of $V$, so $V$ has $d_{\text{model}}$ rows and two columns.

The second expression reads the activation. A plain inner product $\langle v_s, h \rangle$ will not do, because the lens vectors are not orthogonal to each other: part of whatever lies along $v_t$ would show up in the source reading. The [[pseudoinverse]] $V^\dagger$ solves the least-squares problem instead. It returns the pair of weights $c$ for which $Vc$ is the closest point in $\text{span}\{v_s, v_t\}$ to $h$ — one number for how much source is present, one for how much target.

The third expression writes the edit back. $\sigma$ exchanges the two entries, sending $c = (c_1, c_2)$ to $(c_2, c_1)$. Multiplying the coordinate change by $V$ turns it back into a residual-stream vector, which is added to $h$:

$V(\sigma(c) - c) = (c_2 - c_1)\,v_s + (c_1 - c_2)\,v_t.$

The amount of source present is subtracted, and the same amount of target is added. Scaling the difference by [[swap-strength-alpha]] doubles both halves of that trade at $\alpha = 2$.

The orthogonal component follows from the algebra. Writing $h = Vc + r$ with $r$ orthogonal to the two vectors gives $h_{\text{patched}} = V\sigma(c) + r$: only the two coordinates move, and $r$ survives intact.

The swap is applied at every token position across a band of middle layers and held there, a setting the paper calls clamping. On 50 two-hop prompts it moves the target answer to top-1 on 54% of trials for Haiku 4.5 and 70% for Sonnet 4.5.

terms.definition: The activation being edited: the residual-stream vector at one layer and one token position of the forward pass, before the intervention.
The activation after the swap, written back into the forward pass in place of $h$. It differs from $h$ only within the plane spanned by the two lens vectors.
The vocabulary token naming the concept being removed — the one the model is actually representing at that position, for example France or spider.
The vocabulary token naming the concept being written in, for example China or ant. Here $t$ indexes a token in the vocabulary, not a position in the prompt.

The J-lens vectors for the source and target tokens at this layer: the rows of $W_U J_\ell$ for those tokens, each a residual-stream direction associated with the model's disposition to say that token.
The matrix whose two columns are the source and target lens vectors. Multiplying a coordinate pair by $V$ turns it into a residual-stream vector in the plane those two directions span.

The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $V$. Because $V$ is tall and its columns are not orthogonal, this is what recovers the correct coordinates rather than a plain projection onto each vector separately.
The notation for the pseudoinverse. It marks $V^\dagger$ as the least-squares generalization of a matrix inverse to a non-square matrix.
The lens coordinates: a pair of numbers giving how much of $h$ lies along $v_s$ and how much along $v_t$, in the least-squares sense of $V^\dagger h$.
The permutation that swaps the two entries of $c$, optionally with a scale factor. It is the whole content of the intervention: nothing else about $c$ changes.
The change in lens coordinates the swap requires. Multiplying it by $V$ converts that change back into a residual-stream vector to add to $h$.
An optional multiplier on the swap's magnitude, scaling how far the coordinates are pushed. The default is a plain exchange; $\alpha = 2$ subtracts the source and adds the target at double strength.
The two-dimensional plane through the origin containing all combinations of the two lens vectors. It is the only part of activation space the swap touches.
The part of $h$ perpendicular to that plane, written $r$ in the walkthrough. It carries everything else the activation represents and passes through the intervention unchanged.

Holding the swapped coordinates at their new values at every position and layer in the affected band throughout the forward pass, rather than editing once and letting later layers restore the original values.
The Jacobian lens: the per-layer matrix $J_\ell$ whose composition with the unembedding supplies the vectors $v_s$ and $v_t$ used here.
The simpler write operation the paper contrasts with the swap: adding a scaled lens vector to inject a concept, without removing anything.
The width of the residual stream. It is the number of rows of $V$ and the length of $h$, $v_s$ and $v_t$.

numbers.meaning: The number of columns of $V$, and so the number of entries in $c$. The swap is defined for exactly one source concept and one target concept, which is what makes $\sigma$ a simple exchange of two numbers.
The shape of $V$: one row per residual-stream dimension, one column per lens vector. Because it is tall, it has no ordinary inverse, which is why the pseudoinverse appears.

The plain swap, in which the source coordinate is replaced by the target coordinate and vice versa. This is what $\sigma$ does when no scale factor is named, and it is the setting reported unless the paper says otherwise.

The 'double strength' swap: the source lens vector is subtracted and the target added at twice the magnitude the plain exchange would use. The paper introduces it because the plain swap sometimes leaves the source concept still dominant.

Successful swaps at the default strength in the flexible-generalization experiment: 16 function templates times 12 source-target pairs each. Success means the target-appropriate answer reaches top-1 in the model's output.

Successful swaps in the same experiment at $\alpha = 2$. Doubling the strength converts 25 further trials, which the paper reads as evidence that many failures were partial swaps rather than absent effects.

Swap success on 50 two-hop factual prompts for Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5 respectively: the fraction of trials in which exchanging the unspoken intermediate's coordinates moves the target-appropriate answer to the top of the output distribution.
The number of two-hop factual prompts with known unspoken intermediates in that systematic evaluation, with each swap target drawn at random from the same category as the true intermediate.
